title: Older adults are missing from Maryland’s SNAP conversation
summary: There's been a lot of talk about SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program recently, but one voice has been noticeably absent, writes Stephanie Archer-Smith -- the older Marylanders for whom the program can mean so much.
content:
by Stephanie Archer-Smith, Maryland Matters December 28, 2025

by Stephanie Archer-Smith, Maryland Matters December 28, 2025

Maryland’s recent efforts to soften the impact of SNAP delays and federal restrictions are important and appreciated.

But this moment exposes a deeper truth we cannot ignore: Older adults are routinely left out of the decisions that shape their lives, even when those decisions determine whether they have enough food to eat.

At Meals on Wheels of Central Maryland, we see the consequences every day. There is a growing gap for homebound aging adults, particularly those ages 55-64. Many live with chronic illness or disability and cannot “make do” when benefits are cut.

Yet they are often absent from policy conversations, even when they are directly affected.

The SNAP reductions make this painfully clear. When benefits drop for older adults, they do not adjust their budgets — they go hungry. They skip meals. They ration medication. They decline. And when they inevitably fall into crisis, the cost shifts to emergency departments, long-term care, and community organizations like ours.

Meals on Wheels of Central Maryland delivers 1.4 million meals each year to homebound, medically fragile older adults. We enter their homes. We see the desperation that rarely shows up in reports.

As Maryland responds to these federal changes, we urge leaders to include older adults from the outset. Supporting home-delivered meals and similar interventions is not optional. It is essential if we want older Marylanders to remain safe, nourished, and living with dignity-rather than becoming invisible casualties of systems not designed with them in mind.
